name: Dutch East India Company
anchor: Batavia, now Jakarta, the company's headquarters on Java.
founder: Dutch trading firms merged by the States General
stopped_by: Bankruptcy, and the charter was allowed to expire
currency: The company struck its own coins
laws: Company justice under its charter, including execution of convicts
challenge: Fourth Anglo-Dutch War of 1780 and bankruptcy
recognition: Dutch charter; treaties with Asian rulers
story:
The Dutch East India Company, known by its Dutch initials VOC, was a trading company that also ruled territory. A charter is a document in which a government grants a company special rights. On 20 March 1602 the States General, the assembly of the Dutch Republic, merged several existing trading firms into one company and gave it a 21-year monopoly on trade east of the Cape of Good Hope and west of the Strait of Magellan.
The company could do things normally done by a state. It could wage war, negotiate treaties, strike coins, build forts, keep armies, found colonies, and imprison and execute convicts. Its investors could lose only the money they had paid in. A governor-general, a post created in 1610, ran its affairs in Asia with a Council of the Indies to advise and check him, and 17 directors in the Netherlands, the Heeren XVII, kept formal overall control.
On 30 May 1619 Jan Pieterszoon Coen stormed Jayakarta on Java and founded Batavia on its ruins as the company's headquarters. The company conquered the Banda Islands between 1609 and 1621. About 15,000 people lived there before the conquest, and about 14,000 of them were killed, enslaved or fled. Its holdings came to include Ceylon, Malacca, the Malabar coast and the Cape Colony in southern Africa.
The Fourth Anglo-Dutch War of 1780 halved its fleet and left its net assets at zero. The board was dismissed in 1796, and the charter was allowed to expire on 31 December 1799. The Batavian Republic, the Dutch state of that time, took over the company's possessions and its debts.
mechanism: A state handed war-making, treaty-making and coinage to a private company by charter. Those powers rested on the grant, and when the company failed the state took over its land and debts.

name: English East India Company
anchor: Calcutta, now Kolkata, where the company set up a base after 1690. Its headquarters was East India House in London.
founder: Merchants of London, chartered by Queen Elizabeth I
laws: Civil and criminal jurisdiction over areas it acquired
challenge: Indian Rebellion of 1857
recognition: English royal charter; sovereignty passed to the Crown in 1858
story:
The East India Company began as a group of London merchants. On 31 December 1600 Queen Elizabeth I gave them a charter, a document granting special rights, with a 15-year monopoly on English trade east of the Cape of Good Hope and west of the Straits of Magellan.
Around 1670 a series of five acts under Charles II gave the company the right to acquire territory on its own, mint money, command forts and troops, form alliances, make war and peace, and hold civil and criminal jurisdiction, meaning the authority to try cases, over the areas it acquired.
On 23 June 1757 at Plassey, Robert Clive's force of about 800 soldiers and 2,200 Indian soldiers known as sepoys defeated Siraj ud-Daula, the Nawab of Bengal, helped by a prior plot with the Nawab's commander, Mir Jafar. In 1765 the Mughal emperor Shah Alam II granted the company the diwani, the right to collect and manage the revenues of Bengal, Bihar and Orissa. The Great Bengal famine of 1770 is estimated to have killed about 10 million people. At its peak the company's three armies totalled about 260,000 soldiers, about twice the size of the British Army at certain times.
By 1858 the company, or princely states tied to it by treaty, ruled most of modern India, Pakistan and Bangladesh along with Lower Burma. It had given up its commercial assets in India in 1833. After the Indian Rebellion of 1857, the Government of India Act 1858 nationalised it, and the Crown took over its possessions, its administration and its armed forces. The company was formally dissolved on 1 June 1874.
mechanism: A company held trading rights from its own state and revenue rights from a local emperor, and it enforced both with its own army. Its home parliament could take all of this over by passing a statute, and in 1858 it did.

name: Royal Niger Company
anchor: Lokoja, at the meeting of the Niger and Benue rivers in Nigeria.
recognition: British royal charter of 1886, with over 400 treaties with local leaders
cost: £865,000 paid by Britain for its territories
story:
The Royal Niger Company grew out of British firms trading on the Niger River in what is now Nigeria. George Goldie argued that the surviving firms should merge, and by 1879 he had helped combine them as the United African Company. It later became the National African Company.
In July 1886 it received a royal charter, a grant of special rights from the British Crown, and became the Royal Niger Company, with Lord Aberdare as governor and Goldie as vice-governor. Over 400 treaties with local leaders obliged local people to trade only with or through the company's agents. British consuls later turned these into general treaties. The company's monopoly and treaties helped Britain resist French and German calls at the Berlin Conference of 1884 to 1885 to open Niger trade to all.
The charter was revoked in 1899. On 1 January 1900 the company transferred its territories to the British government for £865,000. The land, together with the Niger Coast Protectorate, became the protectorates of Northern and Southern Nigeria, which were united as Nigeria in 1914. The business carried on as the Niger Company, then the United Africa Company from 1929, and it came under the control of Unilever in the 1930s.
mechanism: Treaties signed by a private firm with local rulers gave its home state a claim against European rivals. Once the state wanted direct rule, it revoked the charter and paid for the territory.

name: Hudson's Bay Company as a government
aka: The Governor and Company of Adventurers of England trading into Hudson's Bay
anchor: Western shore of Hudson Bay, where the company built its forts.
founder: London investors, with Prince Rupert of the Rhine as first governor
laws: Company-controlled courts, such as the Court of Assiniboia
recognition: English royal charter; sovereignty lay with the Crown
story:
On 2 May 1670 King Charles II gave a royal charter to a group called the Governor and Company of Adventurers of England trading into Hudson's Bay. It granted them sole trade over Rupert's Land, the region drained by all rivers flowing into Hudson Bay. That area was about 3.86 million square kilometres, more than a third of modern Canada, and its exact boundaries were unknown at the time.
For about 200 years the company was the government of that land in practice. It built forts on the bay, and later posts inland, and it set prices through a list called the Standard of Trade, which used a unit called the Made Beaver. It issued its own paper money from 1820 to 1870 and controlled courts, such as the Court of Assiniboia. In 1821 the British government forced it to merge with its violent rival, the North West Company, and a licence then extended its reach to the Arctic Ocean and the Pacific.
In 1869 the company turned down a US offer of 10 million Canadian dollars and agreed to return Rupert's Land to Britain, which passed it to Canada and lent Canada £300,000 to pay the company. The company kept its trading posts and one-twentieth of the fertile land. The Deed of Surrender took effect on 15 July 1870.
The company survived as a retailer. It filed for creditor protection on 7 March 2025, its stores had closed by 1 June 2025, and its royal charter was auctioned in the liquidation.
mechanism: A trade monopoly from the Crown became government in practice because no other authority was on the ground. The sovereignty stayed with the Crown, so the company could give up the land only through Britain.

name: British South Africa Company
anchor: Fort Salisbury, now Harare, where the Pioneer Column stopped in 1890.
stopped_by: Responsible government in Southern Rhodesia in 1923; an agreement ending its rule in Northern Rhodesia in 1924
challenge: Jameson Raid and the Matabele Wars
cost: £4 million paid in 1964 to end its mineral rights
story:
The British South Africa Company was formed by Cecil Rhodes and received a royal charter effective 20 December 1889. A royal charter is a grant of special rights from the Crown. This one first ran for 25 years. It let the company make treaties with African rulers to secure public order, subject to British approval, and form banks, own and grant land, and raise a police force. In return it was to develop the territory, respect African laws, allow free trade and respect all religions.
The company relied on the Rudd Concession, a mining grant obtained from the Ndebele king Lobengula. A group of settlers known as the Pioneer Column reached Fort Salisbury in 1890, and a company Administrator was appointed that October. Company police fought in the First and Second Matabele Wars, and uprisings followed in 1896.
After the Jameson Raid, Rhodes accepted full responsibility and he and Beit, a fellow director, were removed as directors in June 1896. The police were renamed the British South Africa Police and reported from then on to the British High Commissioner, and Britain tightened its oversight of the company.
Company rule ended in Southern Rhodesia in 1923, when that territory gained responsible government, and in Northern Rhodesia on 1 April 1924. The company kept mineral rights in Northern Rhodesia and collected royalties until 1964. On 23 October 1964 it agreed to give them up for £4 million, paid half by Britain and half by Zambia.
mechanism: The charter let a private company raise police and govern, with the British government keeping the right to approve and oversee. Mineral rights outlasted the right to govern by 40 years.

name: Imperial British East Africa Company
anchor: Mombasa, Kenya, the centre of the company's operations.
challenge: Civil war in Uganda in 1892
story:
The Imperial British East Africa Company was a British firm led by the Scottish businessman William Mackinnon. It was incorporated in London on 18 April 1888, and Queen Victoria gave it a royal charter on 6 September that year. A treaty of 1886 had given Germany the coast of what is now Tanzania and left Britain access to the area of Kenya and Uganda. The company worked from Mombasa and its harbour, with an administrative office in Shimoni, about 80 kilometres to the south.
The company sent Frederick Lugard inland to build a fortified post on Kampala Hill in Uganda. A civil war broke out there in January 1892 and Lugard took part on the company's behalf. The cost of the conflict, added to existing trouble over customs, nearly bankrupted the company.
The British government then took over. It declared a protectorate over Uganda in 1894 and formed the East Africa Protectorate, later Kenya, in 1895. A protectorate is a territory run under the protection and control of a stronger state. Dates for the end of the company vary, with administrative rights passing in 1893 and the company listed as defunct in 1896.
mechanism: A chartered company carried the cost of occupying territory until it could not pay, and then its home state took direct control.

name: Gadsden Purchase
anchor: Southern Arizona around Tucson, within the land bought from Mexico.
story:
The Gadsden Purchase was the sale by Mexico to the United States of 76,800 square kilometres of what is now southern Arizona and south-western New Mexico, the land south of the Gila River and west of the Rio Grande. James Gadsden, the US minister to Mexico, negotiated it with Mexico's president, Antonio López de Santa Anna, starting on 25 September 1853, and the treaty was drawn up at the end of that December.
The United States wanted a flatter southern route for a railway to California. The purchase also settled uncertainty about the border. The first price offered was $15 million. The US Senate rejected the original text on 17 April 1854 by falling three votes short of the two-thirds it needed, and then on 25 April passed a revised version by 33 to 12 that cut more than 10,000 square miles and lowered the price to $10 million. Santa Anna accepted the changes.
The land was added to New Mexico Territory, and Fort Buchanan was built to control it. Arizona Territory was created in 1863 and Arizona became a state in 1912. The disputes over slavery stalled a southern railway until the Southern Pacific reached Tucson in 1880 and completed its route in 1883. Mexican opinion of the sale was negative, and Mexican historians still view it critically.
mechanism: Two governments moved sovereignty and a border by treaty for money. People's ordinary legal position changed with the flag, and the treaty needed approval from the US Senate by a two-thirds vote.

name: Alaska Purchase
anchor: Sitka, Alaska, where the transfer ceremony was held.
founder: United States, through William H. Seward
story:
The Alaska Purchase was the sale of Russia's colony in North America to the United States. William H. Seward, the US Secretary of State, and Eduard de Stoeckl, a Russian diplomat, signed the treaty at 4 in the morning on 30 March 1867 after an all-night session. The price was $7.2 million for 1,518,800 square kilometres, about 2 cents an acre. A list of territory purchases gives a slightly larger area.
Russia needed money after its defeat in the Crimean War. The colony was hard to defend and could easily have been taken by British forces from Canada, and the sea otter population it relied on had nearly died out. The US Senate ratified the treaty on 9 April by 37 votes to 2.
The treaty took effect on 18 October 1867, when the Russian flag was lowered at Sitka and the American flag raised. Nearly all Russians left, and most returned home by 1869. Seward estimated about 60,000 inhabitants, of whom about 50,000 were Inuit or Alaska Natives living outside Russian control, so most people there had not been under Russian rule before the sale.
Alaska was run as a department, then a district and then a territory, and it became a state in 1959.
mechanism: A state sold its claim to a colony by treaty. The buyer received what the seller claimed, including authority over Indigenous peoples who had never been under the seller's actual control.

name: Louisiana Purchase
anchor: The Cabildo in New Orleans, where France transferred the city to the United States.
founder: United States, through Robert Livingston and James Monroe
story:
The Louisiana Purchase was the sale by France to the United States of a claim to about 2,140,000 square kilometres of North America, west of the Mississippi River. Robert Livingston and James Monroe signed the treaty for the United States in Paris on 30 April 1803 with François Barbé-Marbois, the French treasury minister.
France had ceded the territory to Spain in a secret treaty of 1762 and got it back in a secret treaty of 1800. Napoleon then gave up on a New World empire because the revolt in Saint-Domingue was not put down and war with Britain looked close. The price was 80 million francs, or $15 million. The United States took on up to $3.75 million of French debts to its own citizens and paid the rest in bonds, which it financed through British and Dutch banks. With interest the cost came to about $23.3 million.
President Thomas Jefferson considered amending the US constitution to allow the purchase, and his cabinet persuaded him that the power to make treaties was enough. The Senate approved the treaty by 24 votes to 7 on 20 October 1803.
The treaty was negotiated without consulting the Native nations living on the land, who had not ceded it to any colonial power. What the United States bought, in effect, was the sole right among outsiders to obtain Indian lands. Later treaties and settlements for those lands cost it about $2.6 billion through 2012.
mechanism: A seller can pass on only what it holds. France sold its claim against other colonial powers, and the people on the land had to be dealt with separately, often through decades of further treaties and force.

name: Sale of the Danish West Indies
aka: Treaty of the Danish West Indies
anchor: Saint Thomas, one of the three islands sold.
story:
In 1916 Denmark sold three Caribbean islands, Saint Croix, Saint John and Saint Thomas, to the United States for $25 million in gold. The treaty was signed in New York on 4 August 1916 by the Danish minister Constantin Brun and the US Secretary of State Robert Lansing. The islands cover about 400 square kilometres. The islands are now the US Virgin Islands.
Earlier deals had failed. A treaty of 1867 for $7.5 million was ratified in Denmark and never by the US Senate. A deal of 1902 for $5 million failed when the upper house of the Danish parliament tied 32 to 32. During the First World War, Americans feared that Germany might seize the islands if it invaded Denmark, and the islands lay close to the Panama Canal.
Danish voters took part in a referendum on 14 December 1916 and the Danish parliament ratified the treaty on 22 December. The islands changed hands on 31 March 1917, now a public holiday called Transfer Day. As part of the deal Lansing declared that the United States would not object to Denmark extending its interests to the whole of Greenland.
mechanism: A sale by treaty that came with a side declaration on a different territory. The islanders' own status was decided by the two governments and voters in Denmark.

name: Mexican Cession
anchor: Guadalupe Hidalgo, near Mexico City, where the treaty was signed.
challenge: Land grant disputes into the 21st century
cost: $15 million plus $3.25 million in debts taken over
story:
The Mexican Cession was the transfer of about 1.36 million square kilometres from Mexico to the United States by the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, signed on 2 February 1848. It ended the Mexican-American War and covered present-day California, Nevada, Utah, most of Arizona and parts of New Mexico, Colorado and Wyoming, about 55 per cent of Mexico's territory.
The treaty mixes a peace settlement with a sale. The United States paid $15 million in yearly instalments of $3 million and took over $3.25 million that Mexico owed to US citizens.
People living there had one year to choose between US and Mexican citizenship, and over 90 per cent chose US citizenship. The treaty protected existing property rights. The US Senate removed the article that would have guaranteed land grants made by Spain and Mexico. A later protocol confirmed those grants under Mexican law, the United States later ignored it, and disputes over them continued into the 21st century.
mechanism: A payment attached to a cession at the end of a war. Private land titles were meant to survive the change of sovereign, and their protection depended on the buyer's Senate and courts.

name: Sale of Florida
anchor: Northern Florida, within the land transferred.
founder: United States, through John Quincy Adams, and Spain, through Luis de Onís
cost: About $5 million paid to US claimants
story:
Under the Adams-Onís Treaty, signed in Washington on 22 February 1819, Spain gave East and West Florida to the United States. John Quincy Adams negotiated for the United States and the Spanish ambassador, Luis de Onís, for Spain. The treaty also drew a border running from the Gulf of Mexico to the Pacific.
The money did not go to Spain. The United States agreed to compensate its own citizens for losses they said Spain had caused, and a commission paid out about $5 million before it closed in 1824. A list of territory purchases counts this as the price of about 200,000 square kilometres.
The US Senate approved the treaty unanimously two days after signing. Spain delayed until October 1820, the Senate voted again, and the treaty took effect on 22 February 1821.
mechanism: A cession paid for by cancelling claims. The buyer settled debts owed to its own citizens, so the sale could be counted as a purchase with no cash passing to the seller.

name: Cession of the Philippines
anchor: Manila, Philippines.
challenge: The First Philippine Republic resisted American sovereignty
story:
By the Treaty of Paris, signed on 10 December 1898 after the Spanish-American War, Spain ceded the Philippine Islands to the United States for $20 million. The islands cover about 300,000 square kilometres.
Spain's hold was already contested. Philippine revolutionaries had declared independence from Spain on 12 June 1898. Felipe Agoncillo, a lawyer representing the First Philippine Republic, was denied any part in the talks.
Fighting between Filipino and American forces broke out in Manila on 4 February 1899. Two days later the US Senate approved the treaty by 57 votes to 27, just above the two-thirds needed. The treaty took effect on 11 April 1899.
mechanism: Two outside states set the sovereignty of a territory by treaty and left out the government its people had declared. Recognition by those two states did not settle the matter on the ground, which went to war.

name: Sale of Saint Barthélemy
anchor: Gustavia, Saint Barthélemy.
story:
Saint Barthélemy is a Caribbean island of 21 square kilometres that passed between owners several times. The Order of Saint John, a Catholic knightly order, held it in the 1600s, and the French West India Company bought it in 1665 with the order's other Caribbean holdings.
In 1784 King Louis XVI of France traded the island to Sweden for trading privileges in Gothenburg. The Swedes named the town of Gustavia after their king, Gustav III, and made it a free port, one where goods paid no customs duties. The colony lasted nearly a century.
After a status referendum in 1877, Sweden sold the island back to France, and it returned on 16 March 1878. A list of territory purchases gives the price as 320,000 French francs. Today it is a French overseas collectivity, a territory with its own council that remains part of France. It separated from Guadeloupe in 2007 and left the European Union in 2012. The 2023 census counted 10,660 residents.
mechanism: A small territory moved between states by trade and by sale, with a local vote before the second transfer. Later changes to its status came through French law.

name: Transfer of Gwadar to Pakistan
anchor: Gwadar, on Pakistan's Arabian Sea coast.
founder: Pakistan and the Sultanate of Muscat and Oman
cost: Accounts differ: 5.5 billion Pakistani rupees, or a contribution of about $3 million
story:
Gwadar is a port town on the Arabian Sea. It was an overseas possession of the Sultanate of Muscat and Oman from 1783 to 1958, a link that began with a grant from the Khan of Kalat to Sultan bin Ahmad.
On 8 September 1958 Oman handed Gwadar to Pakistan. Prime Minister Feroz Khan Noon and his wife, Viqar-un-Nisa Noon, are credited with convincing the British government to allow the handover. Sources disagree on the money. One Wikipedia list gives a price of 5.5 billion Pakistani rupees and an area of 15,210 square kilometres, and Wikipedia's article on Gwadar gives no official price and mentions a contribution of about $3 million from Prince Karim Aga Khan IV.
Gwadar became part of Makran district and a district of its own in 1977. Construction of the first phase of Gwadar Port began in 2007 at a cost of $248 million, and in 2013 the state-owned China Overseas Port Holdings acquired the port.
mechanism: A state transferred an overseas possession by agreement for money, with a third state's consent. Later the buyer gave a foreign state-owned company the port, which involves control of a business and leaves sovereignty with Pakistan.

name: Return of Elten and Selfkant
anchor: Elten, on the Rhine near Emmerich, Germany.
story:
After the Second World War the Netherlands took small pieces of German land. On 23 April 1949 Dutch troops occupied about 69 square kilometres, with almost 10,000 inhabitants in all. The largest parts were the town of Elten on the Rhine, with 3,235 people, and Selfkant near Sittard, with 5,665.
West Germany began negotiating for their return in March 1957. A treaty signed in The Hague on 8 April 1960 had West Germany pay 280 million German marks for the return of Elten, Selfkant and the village of Suderwick. The payment was described as compensation. The land went back on 1 August 1963, except for a hill of about 3 square kilometres near Wyler that the Netherlands kept.
Before the border moved, traders stored coffee and butter in the towns about to change country. At midnight the goods were on the other side of the border without having paid import tax. The night is remembered as Butter Night. It is the most recent sale in a Wikipedia list of territory purchases.
mechanism: Land taken after a war was returned by treaty for a payment. It shows that a border change also moves customs and tax law in a single instant.

name: Shenzhen Special Economic Zone
anchor: Shenzhen, southern China.
founder: Government of China under Deng Xiaoping
laws: Authorised to develop local legislation under China's system
recognition: Created by China inside its own territory
story:
A special economic zone is an area of a country where the government applies lighter rules on tax and trade in order to attract investment. Shenzhen, in southern China, became one in 1980. It was one of four such zones set up that year and the first created under Deng Xiaoping. Before 1980 the area had about 310,000 residents.
Investors received tax incentives tied to property deals, lower labour costs and easy trade rules. The zones were also authorised to develop their own legislation, and Shenzhen was the most active in legal experiments between 1979 and 1990. Until 2010 the zone covered four districts totalling 493 square kilometres, and in 2010 it was extended to the rest of the city.
The population reached 4.33 million by the end of 2000. The official count in 2007 was 8.6 million, and the true figure may have been 12 to 14 million. The zone is governed by the Shenzhen Municipal People's Government, which is part of the Chinese state.
mechanism: The central state granted a place freedom to try different economic rules and write local laws. The state set up the grant and remains the government there, so it gives no separate territory.

name: Jebel Ali Free Zone
anchor: Jebel Ali, about 35 km south-west of Dubai city.
founder: Emirate of Dubai under Sheikh Rashid bin Saeed Al Maktoum
story:
A free zone is an area where companies get special tax and customs rules. Jebel Ali, about 35 kilometres south-west of Dubai city, began with a port that opened in 1979 by decree of Sheikh Rashid bin Saeed Al Maktoum, Dubai's ruler. The aim was to widen Dubai's economy beyond oil. The port, operated by DP World, is described as the largest man-made harbour in the world.
The Jebel Ali Free Zone was set up around the port in 1985. Companies that move there reportedly get 50 years without corporate tax, no personal income tax, no import or re-export duties, no currency restrictions and easier hiring of workers through authorised companies.
The zone has over 8,700 companies from more than 100 countries and accounts for about 23 per cent of Dubai's economic output. It is a part of the Emirate of Dubai and has no separate political status.
mechanism: A government offers tax and customs exemptions inside a fenced commercial area. The exemptions are the government's own to give, and the area stays under that government.

name: Shannon Free Zone
anchor: Next to Shannon Airport, County Clare, Ireland.
story:
The Shannon Free Zone is a business park of 2.43 square kilometres beside Shannon Airport in the west of Ireland. It was set up in 1959 on a proposal by Brendan O'Regan, the airport's director, and is described as the world's first modern free-trade zone, an area with lower taxes and customs barriers to draw foreign firms.
Businesses there received tax incentives on staff and profits until 2003, plus tariff reductions. Shannon Development, an Irish government agency, managed it until 2014, and a semi-state company has managed it since. In 2019 more than 100 international firms employed more than 8,000 people there.
The model travelled. Shannon influenced China's special economic zones, and Chinese leaders including Jiang Zemin, in 1980, Wen Jiabao and Xi Jinping have visited it. Many of the original tax incentives have since ended, and it carries on as a business park under ordinary Irish law.
mechanism: A government agency ran a zone offering tax and tariff breaks. Because the breaks came from Irish policy, they could be withdrawn, and many were.

name: Masan Free Trade Zone
anchor: Masan, now part of Changwon, South Korea.
laws: A special act of the Korean parliament
story:
The Masan Free Trade Zone is an industrial area in southern South Korea. It was designated in 1970 as the country's first foreign investment zone, under a law setting up free export zones, Act No. 2180. A free export zone is an area where firms can make goods for sale abroad on special terms.
From the 1970s to the 1990s the zone accounted for more than 4 per cent of Korea's exports. Its governing law was replaced by a free trade zone act in 2000, and the zone was renamed accordingly. It marked its 50th anniversary in 2020.
It was the only one of Korea's seven free trade zones not designated as an industrial complex, which kept its building limits low and shut it out of national support projects. Korea's National Assembly passed an amendment to convert it into a national industrial complex, raising the share of land that may be built on from 70 to 80 per cent.
mechanism: A zone created and repeatedly rewritten by ordinary acts of parliament. Its rules last as long as the parliament keeps them.

name: Neom
anchor: Tabuk Province, Saudi Arabia, at the northern tip of the Red Sea.
founder: Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman; Public Investment Fund
laws: Promised own tax and labour laws and an autonomous judicial system
challenge: Howeitat people resisted eviction; three were sentenced to death in 2022
recognition: Inside Saudi Arabia, wholly owned by its state fund
cost: $1.6 trillion first estimated; over $8.8 trillion by 2025
story:
Neom is a planned development of 26,500 square kilometres in north-west Saudi Arabia, announced by Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman on 24 October 2017. It is run by a company set up in 2019 and wholly owned by the Public Investment Fund, the Saudi state's investment fund. The first cost estimate was $1.6 trillion, and by 2025 the estimate had grown to over $8.8 trillion.
The crown prince said Neom would operate independently of the existing government framework, with its own tax and labour laws and an autonomous judicial system. The best-known part, The Line, was announced in January 2021 as a city 170 kilometres long and 500 metres high for 9 million people.
About 20,000 people were expected to be moved. In April 2020 Abdul Rahim al-Huwaiti, of the Howeitat people, said security forces were trying to evict him, and he was then shot dead by those forces. They said he opened fire, and his family disputes that. In October 2022 the Specialized Criminal Court sentenced three members of the Howeitat to death for resisting displacement.
By 2025 The Line had been substantially scaled down or suspended, no new contracts were reported that year, and contracts were cancelled in March 2026. An island resort, Sindalah, opened in October 2024 and remained closed to the general public in 2025.
mechanism: The promise of separate law comes from the state that owns the project. A zone like this can change Saudi rules for investors, while the same state keeps its courts and security forces in place, as the Howeitat cases show.

name: Eko Atlantic
anchor: Reclaimed land off Bar Beach, Victoria Island, Lagos.
founder: South Energyx Nigeria, of the Chagoury group
pop: Few buildings by 2020; at least 250,000 planned
laws: Planned as a separate municipality with its own bureaucracy
challenge: Residents blame it for worse coastal erosion and ocean surges
recognition: Inside Nigeria, in partnership with Lagos State
story:
Eko Atlantic is a private city being built on land reclaimed from the Atlantic Ocean at Lagos, Nigeria. Reclamation means making new dry land by pouring sand into the sea. The developer is South Energyx Nigeria, a company of the Chagoury group, which was founded in 2003. About 9 square kilometres are being reclaimed in front of Bar Beach, behind a long sea wall, at a reported cost of about $6 billion.
It is a partnership in which private investors pay, the Lagos State government is a partner and the federal government gives support. Plans say the city will have its own bureaucracy, be treated as a separate municipality and include an offshore banking zone, and that it will provide its own water, waste handling, security, transport and power.
At least 250,000 residents are planned. As of November 2020 only a few buildings were complete, the best known being the Eko Pearl Towers.
Nearby residents say the project has made erosion and ocean surges worse, and critics say the state failed to involve them. In August 2012 a surge swept 16 people into the ocean and killed several. An opposition party blamed the sand filling and called for the project to stop.
mechanism: A company builds new land and supplies services a city government would normally supply, under an agreement with the state. The land lies under Nigerian law and within Lagos.

name: Nkwashi
anchor: About 36 km east of Lusaka, Zambia.
founder: Thebe Investment Management, led by Mwiya Musokotwane
story:
Nkwashi is a private new town planned on 3,100 acres of former ranch land about 36 kilometres east of Lusaka, Zambia. It is being developed by Thebe Investment Management, a Zambian firm launched in 2014 by Mwiya Musokotwane and his father, Situmbeko Musokotwane, a former finance minister.
The firm sells plots and leaves buyers to build their own houses to approved designs. In 2017 plots cost from $12,000 to $80,000. Zambian mortgage rates were often above 27 per cent, so the firm offered payment plans and carried the risk of non-payment itself. About a third of 9,460 residential plots had been sold by then, none had been developed, and 22 kilometres of roads had been built. The plan is for up to 100,000 residents, two man-made dams, schools and a business park.
As of 2023 it was listed among charter city projects in Sub-Saharan Africa. A charter city is a new city given its own special legal rules. Whether Nkwashi holds any such powers is not known, and the developer's described plan is a land sale under ordinary Zambian law.
mechanism: A private company buys land, plans it and sells plots under ordinary Zambian law. It runs private services such as sanitation.

name: Ciudad Morazán
anchor: Caraos community, Choloma, Cortés, Honduras.
laws: Regulations written by the developer, many copied from Próspera
challenge: Honduras repealed the ZEDE law in 2022 and its Supreme Court ruled against ZEDEs in 2024
recognition: A ZEDE under Honduran law, since repealed and ruled unconstitutional
cost: Rents of about $83 to $125 a month in 2021
story:
Ciudad Morazán is a small private town of 24 hectares near Choloma, an industrial area of northern Honduras. It was created by Massimo Mazzone, an Italian businessman based in Honduras, as a ZEDE, or Zone for Employment and Economic Development. Honduras amended its constitution in 2013 to allow these highly autonomous zones, which could write their own rules. The project was approved in 2019, and Mazzone says its permit came in April 2020.
It was aimed at Honduran factory workers and single mothers, and it rents out homes without selling them. In 2021 townhouses were expected to rent for about $125 a month and studios for about $83. One owner leases all spaces, leases run for three months and need not be renewed if a tenant causes problems, and no elected body governs it. Mazzone copied many regulations from Próspera, the larger ZEDE. Plans included an internal police force, a perimeter wall and a panic-button app.
The plan projected 9,000 residents and about 200 lived there in 2023. In April 2022 the Honduran Congress unanimously repealed the ZEDE law, and in 2024 the Supreme Court nullified the constitutional changes behind it. An account published after those rulings said Ciudad Morazán was continuing to operate, while Próspera pursued an $11 billion arbitration claim against Honduras.
mechanism: A national constitution was amended to permit a zone with its own regulations, then a later congress and court removed that basis. Residents' leases work as the rules, with a landlord in place of a government.

name: Songdo International Business District
anchor: Reclaimed land off Incheon, South Korea.
challenge: In 2003 Birds Korea called for a halt over lost tidal flats
recognition: Part of South Korea's Incheon Free Economic Zone
story:
Songdo is a new district of about 600 hectares built on land reclaimed from the Yellow Sea off Incheon, South Korea. Reclaimed land is land made by filling in the sea. Construction began in 2003, with the first target for completion in 2015 and the present one in 2030. A company, New Songdo International City Development, owns or develops it.
Songdo lies in the Incheon Free Economic Zone, one of the areas where South Korea offers special terms to attract business. It is designed as a smart city, with computers built into buildings and streets, a pneumatic system in place of garbage trucks and more than 40 per cent of the area kept as green space. It has about 167,000 residents and hosts the UN Green Climate Fund, chosen in October 2012.
Critics have pointed to its car-centred design and have called some of its sustainability claims greenwashing. In 2003 Birds Korea asked for reclamation to stop because of the loss of tidal flats.
mechanism: A private developer builds a city inside a government economic zone. People there live under South Korean law and the rules of Incheon.

name: Bonifacio Global City
anchor: Former Fort Bonifacio, Taguig, Metro Manila.
founder: Bases Conversion and Development Authority, with Metro Pacific, later Ayala Land and Evergreen Holdings
challenge: Makati and Taguig fought over jurisdiction until 2023
story:
Bonifacio Global City is a business district in Metro Manila built on a former army base. The land was US military property, passed to the Philippine government in 1949 and became the army's headquarters, Fort Bonifacio, in 1957.
A 1992 law created the Bases Conversion and Development Authority to turn old bases into commercial land. In 1995 Metro Pacific Corporation won the bidding at $1.6 billion for 535 acres, and on 3 February that year the authority and a Metro Pacific group formed the Fort Bonifacio Development Corporation. The private group held 55 per cent and the state authority 45 per cent. In 2003 Ayala Land and Evergreen Holdings bought the controlling stake. That company handles the master plan and upkeep.
A private estate company still sits under ordinary local government, and two cities fought over which was in charge. Taguig sued Makati in 1993. On 1 December 2021 the Supreme Court made permanent an order barring Makati from exercising jurisdiction over the area, and in April 2023 it rejected Makati's appeal, which left Taguig in charge.
mechanism: A state sold most of a public asset to a company, kept a minority share and left planning and upkeep to the company. Which city governs it remained a question for the courts.

name: Abu Dhabi Global Market
anchor: Al Maryah Island, Abu Dhabi.
laws: English common law applied directly, with its own courts for civil and commercial matters
recognition: Set up inside the United Arab Emirates
story:
Abu Dhabi Global Market is a financial centre on Al Maryah Island in Abu Dhabi. It was established in 2013 and began work in October 2015. In 2023 a UAE cabinet resolution added Al Reem Island, for a combined area of over 14 million square metres.
Common law is the system used in England, built largely from past court decisions. This zone applies English common law directly, including decisions from England and Wales, without translating it into local statutes. It is described as the only jurisdiction in the region to do so. Its own courts have exclusive authority over civil and commercial matters in the zone.
The zone has its own financial regulator, its own company registrar and its own administrative authority. The stated authority of its courts covers civil and commercial matters.
mechanism: A state uses its own law to switch on a foreign legal system inside a small area for business disputes. The grant covers commerce and finance, and it depends on the host.

name: Astana International Financial Centre
anchor: Astana, Kazakhstan.
laws: Common law court for civil and commercial disputes
recognition: Set up inside Kazakhstan by a constitutional statute
story:
The Astana International Financial Centre is a business zone in the capital of Kazakhstan. Its legal basis, a constitutional statute, was approved on 7 December 2015, and it was launched on 5 July 2018.
Kazakhstan otherwise uses a civil law system, in which judges mainly apply written codes. The centre has a common law court, in which past decisions carry weight, for civil and commercial disputes arising from the centre, and for other disputes where all parties agree in writing. It also has an arbitration centre, where parties can settle disputes privately, and an independent financial regulator. Licensed financial firms are exempt from corporate income tax and VAT.
Placing a common law court inside a civil law country has drawn strong criticism within Kazakhstan.
mechanism: A statute carves out a separate commercial court and tax regime for firms inside a zone. The zone's authority is limited to matters tied to the centre or agreed by the parties.

name: Jamshedpur
anchor: Jamshedpur, Jharkhand, India.
challenge: A 2005 plan for a municipality met residents' protests
story:
Jamshedpur is an Indian city that grew around a Tata Steel plant. Dorabji Tata chose the site near the village of Sakchi for the steel city planned by his father, Jamshedji Tata. Building started in 1908, the first steel ingot was rolled on 16 February 1912, and the city received its name in 1919.
Most Indian cities of its size have an elected municipal corporation. Jamshedpur is described as the only city with over a million people in India without one, and the only one whose basic services are looked after by a private company. A body called the Jamshedpur Notified Area Committee is listed as its governing body.
Politicians proposed a municipality again in 2005. A large majority of residents, mainly working people, opposed it and protested outside the deputy commissioner's office, and the proposal did not go ahead. The 2011 census counted 629,659 people in the city and 1,337,131 in the metropolitan area.
mechanism: A company supplies a city's services instead of an elected council. State and national law and courts still apply, so the company's role covers services and stops short of government.

name: Lavasa
anchor: Mulshi valley, near Pune, Maharashtra, India.
founder: Hindustan Construction Company, through Lavasa Corporation
stopped_by: Environmental halt in 2010, then insolvency from 2018
challenge: Ministry of Environment and Forests stop-work order in late 2010
cost: ₹1,814 crore in a 2023 resolution plan, later scrapped
story:
Lavasa is an unfinished private city in the Western Ghats hills near Pune, India, modelled in style on Portofino in Italy. A subsidiary of Hindustan Construction Company developed it, and the plans were unveiled in 2006.
In late 2010 India's Ministry of Environment and Forests ordered building stopped because the project lacked clearances. On 9 November 2011 it gave clearance with conditions, including an end to cutting into hills and the building of a sewage plant. A private developer could own the land, while the national environment rules still applied.
On 30 August 2018 an insolvency court admitted a creditor's petition against the company. An insolvency court decides what happens to a business that cannot pay its debts. In 2023 it approved selling the city to Darwin Platform Infrastructure for ₹1,814 crore. In September 2024 it scrapped that plan and ordered fresh proceedings. The city remains incomplete and is described as abandoned.
mechanism: A company owned the land of a whole town, and national law still applied. A ministry could halt the work, and when debts went unpaid an insolvency court took charge.

name: King Abdullah Economic City
anchor: Red Sea coast, about 100 km north of Jeddah, Saudi Arabia.
story:
King Abdullah Economic City is a privately developed city on Saudi Arabia's Red Sea coast, about 100 kilometres north of Jeddah. King Abdullah announced it in 2005. It covers 173 square kilometres and was developed by Emaar Properties, a Dubai company, with a company listed on the Saudi stock exchange created for the purpose.
The target was 2 million residents, with the first stage finished in 2010 and the whole project in 2020. By 2018 it had 7,000 residents. The Financial Times reported in 2018 that it had not attracted investment or become a logistics and manufacturing centre, and the BBC said in 2026 that the goal of a business and tourism hub had not materialised.
mechanism: A listed company builds and sells a city with state backing. Shareholders own the company while the land remains under Saudi law.

name: GIFT City
anchor: Gandhinagar district, Gujarat, India.
laws: Separate tax and liquor rules inside the zone
story:
GIFT City is a business district in Gujarat, India, announced by the state government in 2007 and covering 359 hectares by the Sabarmati River. About 105 hectares form a special economic zone, an area with its own tax and trade rules. A state-created company runs it, and subsidiaries supply power, water, data links, cooling and waste services.
It houses an International Financial Services Centre, where firms get certain tax exemptions, tax holidays in some sectors and services free of goods and services tax. Critics have compared these terms with tax havens such as Mauritius and the Cayman Islands, and the state calls them a well-regulated tax structure.
Gujarat bans alcohol, and in December 2023 it allowed controlled drinking in GIFT City's restaurants, hotels and clubs for permanent employees and their approved visitors. Selling bottles stays prohibited.
mechanism: A state carves out one district and gives it different tax and even alcohol rules. Each exception is a choice by the state or national government.

name: Tatu City
anchor: Ruiru, Kiambu County, Kenya, about 20 km north of central Nairobi.
challenge: Shareholder court battle, 2013 to 2018
recognition: Special Economic Zone under Kenyan law from 2017
story:
Tatu City is a privately built city of 5,000 acres about 20 kilometres north of Nairobi, Kenya, on what was a Belgian-owned coffee farm. The company Rendeavour acquired the land in 2010 and the project was established in 2011.
On 22 May 2017 a notice in the Kenya Gazette, the government's official journal, declared it a Special Economic Zone, an area where firms receive government tax incentives. In 2019 it was named a project of special importance. It went through a long court fight over shareholder disputes between 2013 and 2018, and a parliamentary lands committee later cleared it of wrongdoing.
By January 2025 more than 100 businesses were there, including Heineken and Naivas, along with two international schools and several housing projects. Kenya counts it as a flagship of its Vision 2030 development plan.
mechanism: A private owner gets tax treatment through a gazette notice from the state. The notice changes taxes and incentives, and Kenyan courts and parliament continued to oversee the project.

name: Itana
anchor: Lekki Free Trade Zone, Lekki peninsula, near Lagos, Nigeria.
founder: Iyinoluwa Aboyeji, Luqman Edu and Coco Liu
laws: Described by its backers as having its own governance within the free zone
cost: $500 million cited for the first phase
story:
Itana, also called Talent City, is a planned charter city near Lagos, Nigeria, on the Lekki peninsula. A charter city is a new city given its own special legal rules. Its founders are the technology executive Iyinoluwa Aboyeji, the developer Luqman Edu and Coco Liu, and its investors include Binance. Edu cited $500 million in construction costs for the first phase.
It sits in the Lekki Free Trade Zone, where the Nigerian government set up more flexible tax rules for companies in 2009. Its promoters describe it as having its own governance and not following all national rules. The one specific rule reported is a digital membership with a yearly fee of $100, which gives future privileges in its business environment.
The project plans for thousands of residents and a central co-working campus for 1,000. As of January 2023 it was under development and intended as a hub for African tech workers outside Lagos.
mechanism: A private developer builds on a state-created free zone and adds membership rules of its own. The freedom from national rules extends only as far as the zone's legal terms.

name: Radio Syd
anchor: International waters between Copenhagen and Malmö.
stopped_by: Swedish law against pirate radio, then erosion in The Gambia
challenge: Swedish bill against pirate radio, June 1962, and jail for Britt Wadner
story:
Radio Syd was a Swedish pop station that broadcast from ships. In the 1950s Swedish state broadcasting limited recorded music, and a station on a ship in international waters sat outside that system. Nils-Eric Svensson, a young Swede who had studied radio in the United States, started it in December 1958 as Skånes Radio Mercur. It leased air time from Radio Mercur, which broadcast from the Panama-registered ship Cheeta between Copenhagen and Malmö.
Britt Wadner, who had worked in marketing at the station, bought it in 1961 and renamed it Radio Syd in 1962. She bought a ship of her own, the Cheeta Mercur, in 1962 and a larger one, the Cheeta II, in 1964. Its FM signal covered the south-west of Sweden.
The Swedish parliament passed a bill against pirate radio in June 1962. Radio Syd kept broadcasting, and Wadner was jailed at least once for breaking Swedish broadcasting law. The ship sat at sea, and its owner lived on land where Swedish law applied.
Cheeta II was later sold and moved to The Gambia, where it sank. The station was set up on land just outside Banjul, broadcasting on medium wave. Its mast fell in September 2002 because of coastal erosion, which ended transmissions, and an arson fire destroyed the building in January 2020.
mechanism: A ship in international waters falls outside a coastal state's broadcasting monopoly. That state can still prosecute its own residents on land, which is how Sweden reached the owner.

name: Laser 558
anchor: International waters in the North Sea, off the Thames Estuary.
founder: Laser Radio, funded by Philip Smyth, with American staff
challenge: UK government chartered ships to monitor it from 9 August 1985
story:
Laser 558 was a pop station on a ship, the MV Communicator, anchored in international waters off the Thames Estuary from May 1984. The ship was registered in Panama through a company called Deka Overseas. Its disc jockeys and managers were American, and it used a pair of 25 kilowatt transmitters on 558 kHz.
BBC research reportedly put its audience at about four million in the UK and a similar number on the continent. On 9 August 1985 the UK Department of Trade and Industry chartered a ship, the Dioptric Surveyor, to watch Laser and Radio Caroline, and it was replaced in November by the Gardline Tracker.
Laser stopped in December 1985 when the ship was impounded over unpaid creditors. It came back on 1 December 1986 as Laser Hot Hits under new owners and closed for good at Easter 1987.
mechanism: A foreign flag and a position outside territorial waters kept the ship beyond ordinary UK enforcement. The monitoring ship and its creditors then worked on what it needed, such as supplies and money.

name: Voice of Peace
anchor: Anchored off the Israeli coast in the eastern Mediterranean.
founder: Abie Nathan and the Peace Ship Foundation
challenge: Nathan was jailed several times for contact with enemy states and the PLO
story:
Voice of Peace was a radio station on a former Dutch cargo ship, the MV Peace, anchored off the Israeli coast. Abie Nathan, a peace activist, founded it with a New York based group, the Peace Ship Foundation. It first went on air on 19 May 1973 to promote peaceful coexistence in the Middle East and was paid for by advertisers, making it Israel's first private operation of the kind.
The Israeli government tolerated the station overall. The state broadcaster started a rival pop service, Reshet Gimel, in May 1976. Nathan himself was jailed several times under laws barring contact with enemy states and the PLO.
After heavy losses and a broken promise of a broadcast licence and a mooring in Jaffa, Nathan closed the station. He sank the ship in international waters on 28 November 1993, after the Oslo accords. The name returned as an online station in 2009.
mechanism: The ship gave a private broadcaster an audience outside a state monopoly. The state answered by starting a competing service and by applying its criminal law to the founder.

name: Radio 270
anchor: International waters off Scarborough, North Yorkshire.
founder: Ellambar Investments, managed by Wilf Proudfoot
challenge: UK law from 14 August 1967
story:
Radio 270 was a pop station on a Dutch-built fishing boat, the Oceaan 7, bought for £2,500 and anchored in international waters off Scarborough, in the north of England. The company behind it, Ellambar Investments, had many small shareholders. Wilf Proudfoot held the largest share and was managing director.
The boat was registered in Honduras in the name of the programme director, Noel Miller, an Australian, which placed it beyond the reach of British authorities. The station first broadcast on 9 June 1966.
The UK's Marine, &c., Broadcasting (Offences) Act 1967 took effect at midnight on 14 August 1967. It made it a crime to manage, fund, support or supply a pirate radio ship from the British mainland. The station closed one minute before that midnight with the national anthem. The ship was sold, and the sale raised about £12,500, which left no significant return for shareholders once creditors were paid.
mechanism: The UK could not easily act against a Honduran ship at sea, so it passed a law aimed at everyone on land who ran, paid or supplied it. The law removed the ship's money and supplies without boarding it.

name: Radio Scotland
anchor: Off Dunbar, on the first of several anchorages.
challenge: Company fined £80 over an anchorage inside territorial waters
story:
Radio Scotland was a pop station on a former lightship, the Comet, fitted out in Guernsey. Tommy Shields created it, and it began on 31 December 1965 on 1241 kHz. The ship had no engine and had to be towed.
The station usually anchored outside territorial waters, the belt of sea next to the coast where a country's law applies in full. It moved between anchorages off Dunbar, off Troon near Arran, off Ballywalter in Northern Ireland and off Fife Ness. Some west coast anchorages were found to be inside territorial waters, and the company was fined £80.
Shields lobbied the government for an exemption from the Marine, &c., Broadcasting (Offences) Act 1967 without success. The station went off air just before midnight on 14 August 1967.
mechanism: Where a ship anchors decides which law reaches it. A short distance inside the line brought a fine, and the 1967 law then cut off support from land.

name: Tektite habitat
anchor: Great Lameshur Bay, Saint John, US Virgin Islands.
founder: US Navy, Department of the Interior, NASA and General Electric
recognition: US government programme in US waters
story:
Tektite was an underwater living quarters used by the US government. General Electric built it from two metal cylinders joined by a flexible tunnel, and the Navy placed it 13 metres down in Great Lameshur Bay, Saint John, in the US Virgin Islands, in 1969 and again in 1970. People inside lived under pressure and worked in the water by day, a method called saturation diving.
On 15 February 1969 four Department of the Interior scientists went down for Tektite I and stayed more than 58 days, a record for a single team at that time. Tektite II in 1970 ran a series of missions of up to 20 days, each with four scientists and an engineer. NASA helped pay for it, to study how teams behave in confined spaces. Mission 6-50, in July 1970, was the first all-female saturation team, led by Sylvia Earle.
The project sat in a US bay and answered to US agencies, so it raised no question of separate territory. Afterwards the habitat was stored by General Electric, sold for $1 and displayed in San Francisco, and it was dismantled in 1991.
mechanism: A state-run habitat in the state's own coastal waters. Living under the sea changed the engineering, and the law on the surface above continued to apply.

name: Hydrolab
anchor: The Bahamas, plotted approximately. It later moved off Saint Croix, US Virgin Islands.
founder: Part-funded by NOAA, the US ocean and weather agency
recognition: Research station in Bahamian and US waters
story:
Hydrolab was a small underwater research station that could house four people. It was built in 1966 for $60,000 and served as a research station from 1970, funded in part by NOAA, the US government agency for oceans and weather.
It carried out about 100 missions in the Bahamas in the early to mid 1970s and about 80 off Saint Croix in the US Virgin Islands from 1977 to 1985. It was retired in 1985 and put on display at the Smithsonian in Washington, and in 2017 it was at a NOAA science centre in Maryland.
mechanism: A research station worked inside the waters of the Bahamas and then the United States. Its move shows that an underwater habitat takes on the law of whichever coastal waters it is placed in.

name: Helgoland underwater laboratory
anchor: Off the island of Helgoland in the North Sea, Germany.
founder: Biological Institute Helgoland; built by Dräger
challenge: Two divers died in 1969 and one in 1975
recognition: German research project; also used off the USA in 1975
story:
The Helgoland underwater laboratory was a German research habitat built by Dräger in Lübeck in 1968 for the Biological Institute Helgoland. Scientists and technicians lived in it for several weeks, returning to it after each dive and decompressing only at the end of their stay.
It was first placed 25 metres down off the island of Helgoland in 1969. On 6 December that year Karl-Heinz Schumann and a student, Winfried Kreytenberg, died while disconnecting the laboratory from its supply line. It later worked in the Baltic and the North Sea, and in 1975 it was off Rockport in the Gulf of Maine, at 33 metres, for a herring study, during which the German aquanaut Joachim Wendler died of decompression sickness.
Its last use was in 1981. In 1998 the research centre that held it donated it to the German Oceanographic Museum, and it is displayed at the Nautineum in Stralsund.
mechanism: A habitat that worked in several countries' waters with those governments' cooperation. Deep work was possible, with safety resting on the operators and with no separate legal status.

name: MV Narrative
anchor: Brodosplit shipyard, Split, Croatia, which holds the order.
challenge: Refunds of deposits delayed in 2026
recognition: None; ordinary ship registration, Panama listed
cost: Residences from about $600,000 to over $9 million
story:
MV Narrative is a planned ship on which people would buy apartments and live while it sails around the world every three years. The company behind it, Storylines, launched in 2018 and first meant to buy a used ship before switching to a new one. It ordered the ship from the Brodosplit yard in Croatia in 2022, with 547 residences priced from about $600,000 to over $9 million.
Its start date has moved repeatedly, from 2025 to 2026 to 2027. An industry report in February 2025 described no steel cut. In 2026 the company cut its staff and asked people with $10,000 deposits held outside its trust account to wait for their money until a restructuring is finished. It says it has access to a $500 million bank guarantee and is still working out how to turn that into cash.
A residential ship does not create a new jurisdiction. An industry listing gives its flag as Panama, which would mean Panama's law applies on board and each port's law applies when it calls there. A home on board is a purchase from a company, and buyers carry that company's risk.
mechanism: Buying a home on a ship is a private contract with a company, on a vessel under a flag state's law. Until a ship exists, buyers hold a claim for their deposits.

Storylines secures $500M guarantee, second shipyard, refunds in focus, Cruise Industry News

name: Ulyssia
anchor: Monaco, the project's base and planned departure point.
recognition: None; ordinary ship registration, with sources differing on the flag
story:
Ulyssia is a planned residential yacht about 320 metres long, with 122 private homes priced at €10 million to €100 million each. The company, Ulyssia Residences, was founded by the architect Frank Binder and is led by Alain Gruber, a former executive of The World, an earlier residential ship. Binder describes it as the most exclusive club in the world.
Reports differ on key facts. A Monaco Tribune report of September 2025 named Meyer Yachts of Germany as the builder, gave the flag as Switzerland and put delivery in 2030. A later Boat International report named China Merchants Cruise Shipbuilding, with the contract due that November and a first voyage from Monaco in 2031. CruiseMapper lists the flag as the Cayman Islands.
Whichever flag it uses, that country's law would apply on board. More than half the homes were reported reserved in 2025, the condition set for starting construction.
mechanism: A private community on a single ship is a club with a contract. The flag state supplies the law on board, so choosing a flag means choosing an existing legal system.

sources.t: Ulyssia, the world's largest residential yacht, will set sail in 2030, Monaco Tribune
323m residential yacht Ulyssia construction update, Boat International

name: Utopia Residences
anchor: Samsung Heavy Industries' Geoje yard, South Korea, which held the order.
founder: Utopia Residences, financed mainly by the Frontier Group
cost: About $1.1 billion to build; homes from $3.9 million to $36 million
story:
Utopia was a planned residential ship of 108,000 gross tons and 296 metres, with about 190 homes and a hotel, meant to sail around the world. It was announced in 2009, when an order was placed with Samsung Heavy Industries, and was financed mainly by the Frontier Group, a private equity firm. The cost was reported at $1.1 billion, and homes were priced from $3.9 million, rising to as much as $36 million by 2018.
The shipbuilding contract was suspended in 2014 for lack of funding. A new letter of intent in 2017 aimed at delivery in 2022, and that date also passed. Later listings describe it as a dormant concept with no publicly confirmed management and no confirmed funding.
The Bahamas was named as its port of registry, which would have put Bahamian law on board.
mechanism: The ship's flag would have set the law on board. The project stopped at the stage of raising about $1.1 billion.

name: Aleph
anchor: Co-working hub in Palermo, Buenos Aires.
pop: 889 to about 3,000, depending on the count
recognition: None sought; an event under Argentine law
story:
A pop-up city is a temporary community that gathers to live and work together for weeks, using ordinary buildings in an existing city. Aleph ran for about a month in Buenos Aires in August 2024, based around a co-working hub in the Palermo district. It was organised by Crecimiento, a movement that aims to make Argentina a centre of the cryptocurrency industry.
Counts differ. Crecimiento reports about 3,000 attendees, 300 programmers and 70 startups. A research paper counted 889 unique participants, 417 events and 28 days. The Defiant, a crypto news outlet, reported that no more than two dozen people were in the hub's hallways when its writer visited.
Argentine law applied as usual throughout, and the event had no territory. It worked with officials, and a Regulation Day brought in the head of Argentina's securities regulator. A two-week follow-up, Aleph de Verano, was held in December 2024, with more than 1,500 participants, according to Crecimiento.
mechanism: A pop-up city rents space under the host country's law and leaves when the booking ends. Its influence comes from contact with officials, and it gives no legal control of a place.

Behind the scenes in Argentina's crypto scene now that the Aleph pop-up city is over, The Defiant

name: Crecimiento
anchor: Buenos Aires, Argentina.
founder: Crypto entrepreneurs and companies in Argentina
laws: Proposed a regulatory sandbox and a special economic zone; not adopted
recognition: Included in the Buenos Aires Innovation Sandbox programme
story:
Crecimiento, Spanish for growth, is a movement that aims to make Argentina the crypto capital of the world. The idea took shape between February and May 2024 after a group of global crypto leaders visited Buenos Aires. Its partners include Argentine firms such as Lemon and Ripio and international ones such as Protocol Labs and Solana.
It seeks to change the law from inside. A regulatory sandbox is a scheme where firms can try new products under lighter rules for a limited time. With the Cámara Argentina Fintech, Crecimiento proposed one spanning several government agencies, and Buenos Aires included it in the city's Innovation Sandbox programme. It is also working with experts on a proposal for a special economic zone, an area with its own economic rules. By its own account the zone was still under development in early 2025.
It reached senior officials. Its Aleph events drew Demián Reidel, chair of the president's council of advisers, the former president Mauricio Macri and the Buenos Aires mayor Jorge Macri, and it reports over 20,000 people at its events and programmes in 2024.
mechanism: A group builds support among officials to win rules from the government, with a zone as a possible result. Any zone would exist only if Argentina's government chose to pass it.

sources.t: 2024: The Year Crecimiento Took Flight, Crecimiento

name: muChiangmai
anchor: Chiang Mai, Thailand.
recognition: None sought; an event under Thai law
story:
muChiangmai was a pop-up city, a temporary community that lives and works together for some weeks in an existing place, held in Chiang Mai, Thailand, in 2023. A research paper recorded 47 days, 118 events, of which 46 were organised by participants, and 120 unique participants.
Pop-up cities of this kind follow the model of Zuzalu, an invitation-based community. They rent existing buildings and rely on the host city's services, so Thai law applied as usual and the group held no territory.
mechanism: A temporary gathering under the host country's law. People attended on ordinary travel terms and left when it ended.

name: Gathering of Tribe
anchor: Lisbon, Portugal.
recognition: None sought; an event under Portuguese law
story:
Gathering of Tribe was a six-day pop-up community held in Lisbon, Portugal, in 2024. A pop-up city is a temporary community that lives and works together in an existing place. A research paper recorded 364 events, of which 356 were organised by participants, and 151 unique participants, the shortest of the five gatherings it studied.
It held no territory and sought no special legal status, and Portuguese law applied. Who organised it and how it was run beyond these figures is not known.
mechanism: A short gathering under the host country's law, with no claim to separate authority.

name: Benin coup attempt, 1977
anchor: Cotonou, Benin.
founder: Bob Denard and mercenaries, backed by several African leaders
challenge: Condemned by the UN Security Council in Resolution 405
story:
In January 1977 a group of mercenaries led by Bob Denard tried to overthrow Mathieu Kérékou, president of the People's Republic of Benin, by attacking the port city of Cotonou. A mercenary is a soldier hired for pay. The plan was called Operation Crevette, French for shrimp. The date is given as 16 or 17 January.
The attack failed. Denard left documents behind, and they pointed to backing from Omar Bongo of Gabon and Hassan II of Morocco. Jacques Foccart, a French official, denied knowing about the plot and acknowledged that it had support from those two and from Gnassingbé Eyadéma of Togo and Félix Houphouët-Boigny of Ivory Coast. The documents also pointed to the French counsellor René Journiac.
On 14 April 1977 the UN Security Council, after a special mission reported, strongly condemned the attack in Resolution 405 and asked member states to help repair the damage.
mechanism: A private force was paid to change a government, with the plan depending on foreign rulers' backing. Taking a capital by surprise would have won nothing without other states' acceptance, and the UN condemned the attempt.

sources.t: United Nations Security Council Resolution 405, Wikipedia

name: Maldives coup attempt, 1988
anchor: Malé, Maldives.
challenge: Indian intervention within hours
story:
On 3 November 1988 a Maldivian businessman, Abdullah Luthufi, who ran a farm in Sri Lanka, tried to seize the Maldives. A Sri Lankan Tamil armed group, PLOTE, supplied 100 to 200 fighters, who arrived in the capital, Malé, by sea.
President Maumoon Abdul Gayoom appealed for help. India flew about 500 paratroopers from Agra to Malé's airport, and they arrived about nine hours after his appeal. They rescued Gayoom and restored his government within hours. Reported deaths were 19, most of them mercenaries.
Some attackers fled toward Sri Lanka on a hijacked freighter, the MV Progress Light, with hostages. Indian warships caught it and commandos boarded it. In July 1989 India returned the captives to the Maldives for trial. They were sentenced to death, and under Indian pressure Gayoom changed the sentences to life imprisonment.
mechanism: A hired group of 100 to 200 fighters tried to take a small state's capital. The sitting government asked a neighbour for help, and India's intervention came at that request.

name: Operation Gideon
anchor: Near Macuto, La Guaira, Venezuela.
challenge: Six killed; two Americans captured and sentenced to 20 years
cost: $1.5 million retainer in the contract; $212.9 million in an earlier plan
story:
Operation Gideon was a failed sea raid on Venezuela in May 2020 run with a private security company. Silvercorp USA was founded in 2018 by Jordan Goudreau, a former US Army Green Beret. On 16 October 2019 Goudreau signed a General Services Agreement with J. J. Rendón and Sergio Vergara, associates of the opposition leader Juan Guaidó. It set a retainer of $1.5 million. Guaidó denied signing it directly, and Goudreau claimed a seven-page document carried his signature. An earlier plan pitched by Goudreau cost $212.9 million, to be repaid from future oil sales.
About 60 men left Colombia's Guajira Peninsula in two boats on 2 May 2020. The first was sunk near Macuto on 3 May, and six Venezuelan dissidents were killed. The second was intercepted off Chuao after most of its men had been dropped along the shore.
Two former Green Berets, Airan Berry and Luke Denman, were captured, and on 6 August 2020 a Venezuelan court sentenced them to 20 years after they admitted the charges. Venezuela issued warrants for Goudreau, Rendón and Vergara. In June 2023 Cliver Alcalá, a figure linked to the plot, pleaded guilty in the United States to providing material support to a terrorist group and to illegal transfer of firearms.
mechanism: A contract with opposition figures gave a private company no legal authority in Venezuela. Those who took part faced the criminal law of Venezuela, Colombia and the United States.

name: Assassination of Jovenel Moïse
anchor: Moïse's home in Pèlerin 5, Pétion-Ville, Port-au-Prince.
founder: Group including CTU Security and hired former Colombian soldiers
challenge: Arrests in Haiti and trials in Miami
story:
On 7 July 2021, at about 1 in the morning, Haiti's president, Jovenel Moïse, was killed at his home in Port-au-Prince. The attackers numbered 28 foreigners, 26 of them Colombians, of whom at least 21 were former soldiers, and two Haitian Americans. A Miami security company, CTU Security, owned by Antonio Intriago, hired a man to recruit the former soldiers, and its company card paid for 19 plane tickets from Bogotá to Santo Domingo.
Three Colombians were killed in a police shootout, and 18 Colombians and the two Haitian Americans were arrested soon after. Because part of the planning happened in the United States, US law applied. Several people pleaded guilty in Miami and received life sentences, including Rodolphe Jaar, Germán Rivera García and Joseph Vincent. On 8 May 2026 a Miami federal jury convicted Arcángel Pretel Ortiz, Antonio Intriago, Walter Veintemilla and James Solages of conspiring to assassinate him.
In Haiti, 51 people were charged in February 2024. Hearings were paused during the country's gang war and resumed in May 2025. An appeals court later overturned those indictments and ordered a new investigation, and several judges and prosecutors withdrew, some citing their safety.
mechanism: A private company hired former soldiers for an attack on a head of state. Courts in a country where part of the planning took place can try those involved, as US courts did here.

name: The Panama ship register
anchor: Panama City, Panama.
cost: $162 million to the treasury as of December 2015
story:
Every merchant ship is registered with a country and flies its flag. That country's law then applies on board in most matters, wherever the ship sails. Panama's register is run by the state and accepts ships owned by foreigners as well as locals. Registers of this kind are called open registers, and their flags are often called flags of convenience.
It began with Law 63 of 15 December 1917, which let a vessel receive the flag on request. The first ship recorded was the Belén Quezada. Law 8 of 12 January 1925 set out the procedures and formally created the merchant marine registry. Decree-Law 7 of 1998 created the Panama Maritime Authority, which now runs it through about 70 offices around the world.
Panama has been the world's leading flag since 1993. In June 2016 it had about 8,831 ships of about 235 million gross tons, and in 2017 its ships were about 18 per cent of the world fleet. Registration and related activity brought about $162 million to the treasury as of December 2015.
mechanism: A small state makes its sovereign right to register ships available to foreign owners for a fee. Owners get Panama's law on board.
