Panama Ship Registry, Enrique de Alba Arango, Morgan & Morgan

name: Aquapolis
anchor: Off the Motobu Peninsula, Okinawa, Japan.
founder: Government of Japan; designed by Kiyonori Kikutake
recognition: Japanese government pavilion in Japanese waters
story:
Aquapolis was a floating structure built as the centrepiece of Expo '75, a world's fair on the theme of the ocean, held at Okinawa, Japan, from 20 July 1975 to 18 January 1976. The architect Kiyonori Kikutake designed it as a prototype of a community on the sea. A shipyard in Hiroshima built it and it was towed to the Motobu Peninsula. It stood 32 metres high, displaced 28,000 tons and cost about 13 to 14 billion yen, paid for by the Japanese government.
It stayed open as an attraction after the fair. It drew about four million visitors, and as numbers fell it closed in 1993. It was towed to Shanghai in October 2000 to be scrapped.
It was a state project moored in Japanese waters, under Japanese law, with no claim to separate status.
mechanism: A national government built a floating structure in its own coastal waters, so Japanese law applied as on shore. The project tested building methods and raised no legal question of separate status.

sources.t: Expo 1975 Okinawa, Bureau International des Expositions

name: Kikutake's marine city designs
anchor: Japanese coastal waters, plotted off Tokyo as a reference point.
founder: Kiyonori Kikutake and the Metabolism group
story:
Kiyonori Kikutake was a Japanese architect who designed cities on the sea. His best-known design had towers of homes rising from huge concrete rafts that extended into the sea, with fish farms around them. His Ocean City was grouped with towers over 900 feet tall on which living capsules were plugged in like leaves. He also drew a floating colony in 1968 and a floating city for one million people in the 1980s.
About 75 per cent of Japan is mountainous, the flat land floods and the country was crowded after the war. He sought safety from earthquakes, floods and tsunamis. His family had lost land in the land reform of 1947, and he described this work as a kind of protest. In 1960 he helped form the Metabolism group, which proposed buildings that could grow and change, and its manifesto said it was wrong to think that clinging to the land was the surest way to live.
Only Aquapolis at Okinawa, in 1975, came near to building the idea. None of these designs made a claim to stand outside any country.
mechanism: These were designs for extending a country onto the water. They were answers to a shortage of land and made no attempt to leave Japanese law.

name: Green Float
anchor: Equatorial Pacific, plotted as a reference point. No site has been fixed.
story:
Green Float is a concept for a floating city from Shimizu Corporation, a Japanese construction firm, first shown in 2008 as part of its Shimizu Dream series. It imagines a 1,000-metre tower on an artificial island 3,000 metres across, set on the equator in the Pacific, where sunlight is strong and typhoons are few. About 50,000 people would live and work there, with food from a plant factory inside the tower and all power from renewable sources.
The company has made more modest progress with a smaller model. In 2023 Singapore's Economic Development Board reported that Shimizu had developed guidelines for floating structures with the Singapore agency JTC, and that the classification society Nippon Kaiji Kyokai had given approval in principle to Green Float II, about one tenth of the size. A classification society is a body that certifies that a ship or structure is safe. Singapore's interest comes from a need for more land. The scale, start date and costs have not been announced.
No owner, jurisdiction or legal plan for the ocean city is known.
mechanism: The legal path most in view is a smaller structure in a host country's waters, with its approval and under its rules. No legal status has been proposed for an ocean version.

sources.t: Shimizu Corporation's Green Float for a better tomorrow, Singapore Economic Development Board

name: Lilypad
anchor: Open ocean, plotted on the equator as a reference point. The design has no fixed site.
story:
Lilypad is a design by the architect Vincent Callebaut, dated 2008, for a floating city for climate refugees. It has a surface of 500,000 square metres for 50,000 people, with a central freshwater lagoon, three marinas and three artificial mountains, and it takes its shape from the Victoria Regia water lily. It would drift along ocean currents from the equator toward the poles.
The designer's page cites forecasts of sea level rise and an estimate of at least 250 million climate refugees. It also describes the project as a way of extending developed countries' territories offshore, so the city would belong to an existing state. It claims the city would make more energy than it uses, with zero carbon emissions.
The designer's page calls it a prototype and a project. No owner, funding or site is known.
mechanism: A design study that treats the floating city as an offshore extension of an existing country. Its legal status would come from that country or from the flag it flew.
